name: United Arab Emirates
summary: Onshore banks are licensed and supervised by the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE), which publishes its regulations, standards and guidance in the CBUAE Rulebook. The UAE Financial Intelligence Unit receives suspicious transaction reports through goAML, the Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation (EOCN) runs targeted financial sanctions, and the Ministry of Finance is the competent authority for FATCA and CRS. The DIFC and ADGM financial free zones have their own regulators (DFSA and FSRA) and rulebooks; this map covers CBUAE onshore conventional banks only. Explicit staff training duties come from the executive regulations of the federal AML/CFT/CPF law (Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025), the Consumer Protection Regulation, the Fitness and Propriety and Corporate Governance rules for boards, and the 2026 Operational Risk Management Regulation.

regulators.name: Central Bank of the UAE
regulators.role: Licenses, regulates and supervises onshore banks, including AML/CFT/CPF supervision and consumer protection; issues the CBUAE Rulebook.

regulators.name: UAE Financial Intelligence Unit
regulators.role: Receives and analyses suspicious transaction and activity reports filed through goAML and shares financial intelligence.

regulators.name: Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation
regulators.role: Oversees implementation of targeted financial sanctions, maintains list notifications and issues TFS guidance for financial institutions.

regulators.name: Ministry of Finance
regulators.role: Competent authority for FATCA and CRS; receives annual reports from reporting financial institutions and exchanges them with partner jurisdictions.

regulators.name: Dubai Financial Services Authority
regulators.role: Separate free-zone regulator for financial services in or from the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC); not covered by the mappings in this file.

regulators.name: Financial Services Regulatory Authority (ADGM)
regulators.role: Separate free-zone regulator for financial services in or from Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM); not covered by the mappings in this file.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | AML/CFT/CPF Compliance under Decree-Law 10 of 2025
programs.why: Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025, the executive regulations of the 2025 AML/CFT/CPF decree-law, requires banks to run periodic capacity-building programmes for compliance and other relevant staff and makes the compliance officer responsible for ongoing, documented employee training on ML, TF and PF. CBUAE guidance expects induction training, awareness refreshers at least once a year and role-based modules.

references.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (10) of 2025 Regarding Anti-Money Laundering, and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation Financing
references.note: Current federal AML/CFT/CPF law (EOCN copy); repealed Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018. It sets the ML, TF and PF offences, suspicious transaction reporting and the preventive duties of financial institutions (risk assessment, CDD, records, internal policies approved by senior management), leaving the minimum content of those policies, including training, to the Executive Regulations.

references.title: Cabinet Resolution No. (134) of 2025 Regarding the Executive Regulations of Federal Decree by Law No. (10) of 2025
references.note: Implementing regulation (EOCN copy); replaced Cabinet Resolution No. 10 of 2019. Internal policies must include periodic programmes to build the capacity of compliance staff and other relevant employees (Article 21(5)), and the compliance officer must develop, implement and document ongoing training plans for employees on ML, TF and PF and how to combat them (Article 22(4)).

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations Guidelines for Financial Institutions
references.note: Guidance expecting staff screening and training that covers the AML/CFT legal framework, internal procedures and red flags, tailored to customer-facing staff, compliance staff, senior management and the board.

references.title: Best Practices for Licensed Financial Institutions on Implementing Role-Based AML/CFT/CPF Training
references.note: Supervisory best practice: induction training for new joiners, awareness training for all staff at least annually, role-based modules, a training needs assessment, records and testing, with the MLRO reviewing the programme every year.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CBUAE onshore banks)
programs.why: Terrorist financing is an offence under Article 3 of the federal AML/CFT/CPF law, and the employee training duty in the executive regulations covers it. Staff must recognise TF red flags, including small-value flows, charities and cross-border transfers, and know how to escalate them for reporting to the UAE FIU.

CBUAE's 2025 CDD/KYC guidance describes identification, verification, risk rating and when to stop onboarding, which staff must apply consistently.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Politically Exposed Persons under CBUAE PEP Guidance
programs.why: The CBUAE expects banks to identify PEPs, family members and close associates before onboarding, obtain senior approval, establish source of wealth and monitor the relationship. Staff need to apply judgement on PEP status rather than refuse PEPs by default.

references.title: Guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions on the Risks Relating to Politically Exposed Persons
references.note: Expects identification of PEPs, family members and close associates before onboarding, risk rating, senior approval and ongoing monitoring rather than blanket refusal.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Sanctions Compliance and Screening (UAE and UN lists)
programs.why: Banks must screen customers and transactions against the UAE Local Terrorist List and UN Consolidated List and act without delay on matches. EOCN guidance expects ongoing training and awareness for relevant staff and senior management, but no statutory course is prescribed.

references.title: Cabinet Resolution No. (74) of 2020 Regarding the UAE List of Terrorists and Implementation of UN Security Council Resolutions
references.note: Legal basis for targeted financial sanctions. Article 21 requires financial institutions to register for list notifications, screen regularly and on list changes, freeze without delay and without prior notice, notify their supervisory authority of matches and actions, and bar staff from tipping off.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Suspicious Transaction Reporting to the UAE FIU via goAML
programs.why: Banks must report suspicion of ML, TF or PF promptly to the UAE FIU through goAML and must not tip off the customer. CBUAE STR guidance expects staff to recognise and escalate suspicion internally; reporting procedure is part of the AML training programme rather than a separately prescribed course.

references.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (10) of 2025 Regarding Anti-Money Laundering, and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation Financing
references.note: Article 18 requires notifying the FIU without delay through its electronic system when a transaction is suspected; Article 29(1) punishes tipping off.

references.title: Guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions on Suspicious Transaction Reporting

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Unusual Transaction Identification and Escalation

references.title: Guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions on Suspicious Transaction Reporting

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Transaction Monitoring and Alert Investigation
programs.why: Banks need risk-based monitoring systems and documented alert handling. Analysts must be competent to investigate alerts, record rationale and decide whether to file an STR; CBUAE guidance expects specialised training for these roles.

references.title: Guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions on Suspicious Transaction Reporting

audience: Correspondent banking and financial institutions teams
programs.why: The CBUAE treats correspondent relationships as higher risk and describes respondent due diligence, nested account controls and ongoing review. Staff managing these relationships must understand the expectations set in the 2025 guidance.

programs.why: The AML/CFT/CPF law requires banks to keep customer and transaction records for a minimum period and make them available to authorities. CBUAE guidance explains what must be kept and how; staff creating and storing records must follow it.

programs.why: The 2025 framework strengthens senior management accountability for AML failures. CBUAE guidance lists senior management and the board as a training audience, and the Corporate Governance Standards require board induction and ongoing training covering the regulatory environment.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Fraud Prevention, Detection and Reporting
programs.why: CBUAE rules require banks to protect consumer data and assets with an effective control framework and to train staff on it and on reporting breaches, and the code of conduct must prohibit fraud. references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 6: Protection of Consumer Data and Assets

references.note: Supervisors can restrict, suspend or seek replacement of board members and managers responsible for breaches (Article 17), and managers of a legal person can be punished when a crime resulted from their breach of duty (Article 27(5)).

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation and Standards
programs.why: The Consumer Protection Standards require banks to ensure, verify and document that consumer-facing staff and agents are trained and qualified, keep individual training records, close competence gaps promptly and require continuing professional development.

references.title: Consumer Protection Standards

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 5: Business Conduct

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Responsible Financing and Affordability
programs.why: Article 7 of the Consumer Protection Regulation requires banks to assess affordability and suitability before extending credit and to avoid over-indebtedness. Lending staff must be competent to apply these checks.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 7: Responsible Financing Practice
references.note: Requires affordability and suitability assessment before lending and prohibits exploiting customers' circumstances.

references.title: Consumer Protection Standards
references.note: Detailed standards under the Regulation, including verification and documentation that consumer-facing staff are trained and qualified, individual training records and continuing professional development.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Complaint Handling under the Consumer Protection Regulation

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 8: Complaint Management and Complaint Resolution
references.note: Requires an effective complaints process and expects front-line staff to be trained to receive, handle and escalate complaints.

references.title: Consumer Protection Standards
references.note: Detailed standards under the Regulation, including verification and documentation that consumer-facing staff are trained and qualified, individual training records and continuing professional development.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Sanadak Ombudsman and Dispute Resolution
programs.why: Since 2023 consumers can refer unresolved complaints to Sanadak, the CBUAE-established financial ombudsman. Banks must inform customers of this right in writing and cooperate with reviews, so complaints staff must know the process.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 8: Complaint Management and Complaint Resolution
references.note: Requires an effective complaints process and expects front-line staff to be trained to receive, handle and escalate complaints.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Vulnerable Consumers and People of Determination
programs.why: The Consumer Protection Regulation requires banks to train staff at least annually to identify and assist vulnerable consumers and People of Determination, with specialised sensitivity training for staff serving them, and to keep services accessible.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 10: Financial Inclusion
references.note: Requires accessible services for People of Determination and vulnerable consumers, and staff training at least annually to identify and assist them.

references.title: Consumer Protection Standards
references.note: Detailed standards under the Regulation, including verification and documentation that consumer-facing staff are trained and qualified, individual training records and continuing professional development.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Customer Data Confidentiality under CBUAE Consumer Protection Rules
audience: Staff with access to customer data
programs.why: Article 6 of the Consumer Protection Regulation requires employee training and awareness on the bank's data control framework and on reporting security and policy breaches, plus an annual reminder that protecting consumer data is an ongoing duty. Customer account information is confidential and may be disclosed only with consent or legal authority.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 6: Protection of Consumer Data and Assets
references.note: Banks must run employee training and awareness on the data control framework and on reporting security and policy breaches, remind staff yearly of their data-protection duty, and train staff to keep consumer assets secure.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular No. 8/2020)
references.note: Principles-based conduct regime for licensed financial institutions covering disclosure, business conduct, data protection, responsible financing, complaints and financial inclusion.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Debt Collection Conduct
programs.why: The Consumer Protection Standards require written collection policies, discussion of financial difficulty before enforcement where possible, limits on the frequency and manner of contact, and disclosure of collection agents. Collections staff and agents must be competent to follow them.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 5: Business Conduct
references.note: Consumer-facing staff need adequate product knowledge and qualifications; staff giving specific advice need relevant experience and current qualifications; covers fair sales, remuneration and collection conduct.

references.title: Consumer Protection Standards
references.note: Detailed standards under the Regulation, including verification and documentation that consumer-facing staff are trained and qualified, individual training records and continuing professional development.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Sales Practices, Suitability and Qualified Advice
audience: Staff giving financial or investment advice
programs.why: Staff who give specific advice must hold appropriate experience, current knowledge and qualifications, and banks must assess suitability and avoid remuneration that relies mainly on sales volume. This is an express role-based qualification requirement.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 5: Business Conduct
references.note: Consumer-facing staff need adequate product knowledge and qualifications; staff giving specific advice need relevant experience and current qualifications; covers fair sales, remuneration and collection conduct.

references.title: Consumer Protection Standards
references.note: Detailed standards under the Regulation, including verification and documentation that consumer-facing staff are trained and qualified, individual training records and continuing professional development.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 7: Responsible Financing Practice
references.note: Requires affordability and suitability assessment before lending and prohibits exploiting customers' circumstances.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Information Security Awareness for Customer Data
programs.why: CBUAE rules require training and awareness on controls for accessing and handling customer data and on reporting security breaches, and the 2026 Operational Risk Management Regulation requires regular staff training and an awareness role for the risk function. No standalone information security curriculum is prescribed for onshore banks in the sources verified.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 6: Protection of Consumer Data and Assets
references.note: Banks must run employee training and awareness on the data control framework and on reporting security and policy breaches, remind staff yearly of their data-protection duty, and train staff to keep consumer assets secure.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Regulation (Circular No. 1/2026)
references.note: Replaces the 2018 Operational Risk Regulation. Senior management must ensure staff receive regular, appropriate training; the operational risk function designs training and raises awareness; continuity and recovery plans for critical operations are reviewed and tested at least annually.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Data Protection: CBUAE Rules and the Federal PDPL
programs.why: Banking and credit personal data that is protected by its own legislation is carved out of the federal PDPL, so customer data is mainly governed by CBUAE rules, but the PDPL still affects other personal data and cross-border transfers. Staff handling personal data need to know which regime applies.

references.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data
references.note: Federal data protection law. It excludes banking and credit personal data that has its own protective legislation, so banks rely mainly on CBUAE rules for customer data, while the PDPL still matters for other personal data such as employee records and for cross-border transfer limits that the CBUAE references.

references.title: Consumer Protection Regulation, Article 6: Protection of Consumer Data and Assets
references.note: Banks must run employee training and awareness on the data control framework and on reporting security and policy breaches, remind staff yearly of their data-protection duty, and train staff to keep consumer assets secure.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Operational Risk and Operational Resilience (CBUAE Regulation 1/2026)
programs.why: The Operational Risk Management Regulation, in force from September 2026, requires senior management to make sure staff receive regular and appropriate training and gives the operational risk function responsibility for training and awareness. It also requires resilience planning for critical operations.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Regulation (Circular No. 1/2026)
references.note: Replaces the 2018 Operational Risk Regulation. Senior management must ensure staff receive regular, appropriate training; the operational risk function designs training and raises awareness; continuity and recovery plans for critical operations are reviewed and tested at least annually.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Risk Management Regulation and Standards for Banks
programs.why: The CBUAE requires every bank to run a board-owned, bank-wide risk management framework with a risk appetite statement, limits, independent risk, compliance and audit functions, and prompt notice of material breaches. Staff in these functions must understand the framework; no separate course is prescribed. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Risk Management Regulation
references.note: Sets minimum standards for a comprehensive, group-wide risk management approach, with the board ultimately responsible for risk governance and a board-approved risk appetite.

references.title: Risk Management Standards
references.note: Binding companion standards that expand on the regulation, including stress testing and risk data aggregation expectations.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Credit Risk Management Regulation and Standards
programs.why: The CBUAE credit risk rules require a documented framework covering the whole credit lifecycle, from origination and approval through monitoring, recovery and provisioning, with an independent credit risk function. Staff who originate, approve and monitor credit must be competent in it. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Credit Risk Management Regulation
references.note: Requires a documented credit risk framework across origination, underwriting, approval, monitoring, portfolio management, recovery and provisioning, and defines board and credit risk function duties.

references.title: Credit Risk Management Standards
references.note: Companion standards with detailed expectations on limits, collateral valuation, staging and credit models; read together with the regulation.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Liquidity Risk Management under the CBUAE Liquidity Regulations
programs.why: Banks must meet CBUAE liquidity ratios (ELAR or LCR, and stable funding requirements), stress test their liquidity and hold buffers. Treasury, ALM and risk staff need working knowledge of these rules; no specific training is prescribed. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Regulations Re Liquidity at Banks
references.note: Sets the liquidity ratio framework (ELAR or, once approved, LCR) and stable funding requirements for banks.

references.title: J. Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision
references.note: Expects regular liquidity stress testing and a liquidity cushion, and allows the CBUAE to impose higher requirements.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB)
programs.why: The IRRBB rules require banks to measure the effect of rate changes on both earnings and economic value, keep re-pricing schedules and have interest rate models independently validated. Staff running these processes must be competent in them. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Interest Rate and Rate Of Return Risk in the Banking Book Regulation
references.note: Sets minimum IRRBB management requirements, including periodic review and independent validation of the models used.

references.title: Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book Standards
references.note: Mandatory companion standards on measuring earnings and economic value effects and on re-pricing schedules.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Capital Adequacy (Basel III) for UAE Banks
programs.why: CBUAE capital rules set minimum CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios plus conservation, countercyclical and D-SIB buffers, and a Pillar 2 ICAAP reviewed by the CBUAE. Finance, risk and reporting staff must understand them to calculate and manage capital. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Regulations Re Capital Adequacy
references.note: Sets the minimum capital ratios and the capital conservation buffer for banks.

references.title: Standards for Capital Adequacy of Banks in the UAE
references.note: Details the Basel III capital calculations and the countercyclical and D-SIB buffers.

references.title: Guidance for Capital Adequacy of Banks in the UAE
references.note: Explains how banks should apply the capital standards, including the internal capital adequacy assessment.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Model Risk under the CBUAE Model Management Standards
programs.why: The Model Management Standards require banks to tier their models, govern their development and use, and validate them independently; the guidance sets minimum practices for specific model types. Staff who build, validate or rely on models must be competent in these expectations. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Model Management Standards
references.note: Requires a model governance framework with at least two tiers of models by materiality, plus development, validation and use standards.

references.title: Model Management Guidance
references.note: Sets minimum expected practices for credit, IRRBB and other models that banks choose to use.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Large Exposures and Concentration Risk
programs.why: The 2025 Central Bank law lets the CBUAE cap lending to a single person and other operations, and the Large Exposures Regulation sets the limits and reporting. Credit and risk staff must identify connected counterparties and track exposures against the limits. No training duty is stated. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Allows the Central Bank to set operational limits, including the maximum a licensed institution may lend to a single person.

references.title: Large Exposures Regulation
references.note: Defines a large exposure by reference to Tier 1 capital and sets limits for single counterparties and connected groups.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Outsourcing Risk Management for Banks
programs.why: Banks remain fully accountable for outsourced activities and need CBUAE non-objection for material outsourcing. Staff who select and oversee providers must be competent in due diligence, contracts, monitoring and exit planning.

references.title: Outsourcing Regulation for Banks
references.note: Banks remain fully accountable for outsourced activities, need CBUAE non-objection before material outsourcing, and must have continuity arrangements for outsourced services.

references.title: Outsourcing Standards for Banks
references.note: Details due diligence, contract terms, monitoring, exit planning and continuity expectations for service providers.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery
programs.why: The 2026 Operational Risk Management Regulation requires continuity and recovery plans for critical operations, including staff communication arrangements, reviewed and tested at least annually and reported to the board. Staff named in plans must know their roles.

references.title: Operational Risk Management Regulation (Circular No. 1/2026)
references.note: Replaces the 2018 Operational Risk Regulation. Senior management must ensure staff receive regular, appropriate training; the operational risk function designs training and raises awareness; continuity and recovery plans for critical operations are reviewed and tested at least annually.

references.title: Outsourcing Regulation for Banks
references.note: Banks remain fully accountable for outsourced activities, need CBUAE non-objection before material outsourcing, and must have continuity arrangements for outsourced services.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Recovery Planning, Early Intervention and Resolution
programs.why: The 2025 Central Bank law gives the CBUAE early intervention powers, such as ordering a bank to execute measures from its recovery plan, add capital or replace unfit directors, and a full set of resolution powers. Boards and senior management must understand recovery planning and these consequences; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Article 142 lets the Central Bank require a bank in difficulty to apply its recovery plan, raise capital or liquidity, change strategy or management, or appoint interim management; Article 143 sets out resolution powers.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Credit Classification and IFRS 9 Provisioning under CBUAE Rules
programs.why: CBUAE rules tie loan classification to IFRS 9 staging, set provisioning floors and require regular rating reviews, and the 2025 law lets the CBUAE block dividends where provisions fall short. references.title: Credit Risk Management Regulation, Article 9: Classification and Provisioning

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Allows the Central Bank to refuse approval of proposed dividends where provisions are found to be insufficient.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Collateral and Guarantees for Credit Facilities
programs.why: The 2025 law requires banks to obtain and keep adequate guarantees for facilities to individuals and sole proprietors, in line with income and facility size, and bars claims in court where they failed to do so. Lending staff must be competent in collateral and guarantee requirements.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Banks must hold adequate guarantees for facilities to natural persons and sole proprietorships, matched to income and facility size; failing this, claims on those facilities are not admissible and sanctions may follow.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: A bank may not accept its own shares as collateral for customer credit.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Credit Information Reporting to the Al Etihad Credit Bureau
programs.why: Banks supply credit information to Al Etihad Credit Bureau under the Credit Information Law, and the 2025 Central Bank law keeps a CBUAE Risk Bureau that compiles credit data from licensed institutions. Staff who report data or handle disputes must know accuracy, consent and confidentiality rules. The credit information law itself could not be opened.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: The Central Bank Risk Bureau compiles, exchanges and processes credit information from licensed financial institutions under conditions set by the CBUAE board.

references.title: Federal Law No. (6) of 2010 on Credit Information
references.note: Establishes the credit bureau and requires banks and other providers to supply credit information; the legislation portal blocks automated access.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Personal Loans and Consumer Credit Rules
programs.why: CBUAE rules on loans to individuals cap debt burden, loan size and tenor and restrict changes to terms, and the 2025 law bans compound interest on customer facilities. references.title: Regulation No. 29/2011 Regarding Bank Loans and Other Services Offered to Individual Customers
references.note: CBUAE rules for personal loans, overdrafts, car loans and credit cards to individuals, including debt burden, loan size and tenor limits and limits on changing terms.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Banks may not charge interest on accrued interest for customer facilities and must follow CBUAE rules on this.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Mortgage Lending under the CBUAE Mortgage Regulations
programs.why: The mortgage regulations set loan-to-value and debt burden caps, maximum tenor, interest rate stress testing and board-approved lending policies, and the 2025 law lets the CBUAE limit real estate lending. references.title: Regulations Regarding Mortgage Loans

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: The CBUAE board issues regulations limiting credit for real estate purposes.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Wire Transfer Originator and Beneficiary Information Rules
programs.why: The 2025 executive regulations require originator and beneficiary data on international transfers of AED 3,500 or more (verified) and on smaller ones, rules for domestic, intermediary and beneficiary banks, refusal of non-compliant transfers and TFS screening. references.note: Internal controls must include periodic programmes and workshops to build the capacity of compliance staff and other relevant employees.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Fraud Prevention for Digital and Traditional Banking Services
programs.why: The 2025 law requires robust fraud prevention and detection against unauthorised transactions, social engineering and identity theft, prompt customer notification of breaches and cooperation with CBUAE fraud investigations. references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Banks must run robust fraud prevention and detection, notify affected customers promptly of breaches or fraud, report fraud data to the CBUAE on request and apply its preventive measures.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Sexual Harassment Prevention under the UAE Labour Law
programs.why: The UAE labour law prohibits sexual harassment, bullying and violence against workers by employers, managers or colleagues. No statutory training duty was verified, but awareness training is good practice for meeting the prohibition.

references.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (33) of 2021 Concerning Regulating Labor Relations
references.note: Prohibits sexual harassment, bullying and verbal, physical or psychological violence against workers, and requires employers to provide means of protection against workplace injury and occupational disease.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Occupational Health and Safety
programs.why: Employers must provide means of protection against workplace injury, occupational disease and fire risks, and workers must follow safety instructions. No specific bank-sector training obligation was verified.

references.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (33) of 2021 Concerning Regulating Labor Relations
references.note: Prohibits sexual harassment, bullying and verbal, physical or psychological violence against workers, and requires employers to provide means of protection against workplace injury and occupational disease.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Regulatory Reporting to the CBUAE by Qualified Staff
programs.why: The 2025 Central Bank law expressly requires banks to appoint qualified employees to prepare the reports the CBUAE requires, to give them access to the information they need, and lets the CBUAE act against those employees. references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Banks must appoint qualified employees to prepare CBUAE reports and support them with the information needed; the CBUAE may take measures against the bank or those employees.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Banks must file financial position statements and, within three months of year end, audited accounts, the auditors' report and the board report.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Publication of Audited Accounts and Bank Disclosures
programs.why: Banks must publish audited accounts, the auditors' report, board and senior executive names and subsidiaries on their websites and in branches, after CBUAE approval. Finance and secretariat staff must be competent in these disclosure steps.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Banks must publish their audited balance sheet and profit and loss account, the auditors' report, names of directors and authorised individuals, and subsidiaries, on their website and in each branch.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Reports are published within 20 working days of the general assembly, after Central Bank approval.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | UAE Corporate Tax Compliance for Banks

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | FATCA Compliance under the UAE Model 1B IGA

references.title: Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI): FATCA & CRS
references.note: UAE reporting financial institutions must register on the MoF FATCA/CRS system, follow the onboarding and due diligence procedures, and report reportable accounts to the Ministry every year; the Ministry exchanges the data with the IRS and CRS partners.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Common Reporting Standard (CRS) Reporting to the Ministry of Finance
programs.why: The UAE applies the widest approach to CRS: banks must collect self-certifications for new accounts, apply due diligence and report reportable accounts to the Ministry of Finance by 30 June after each reporting year, keeping records for at least five years after the reporting deadline.

references.title: Automatic Exchange of Information (AEOI): FATCA & CRS
references.note: UAE reporting financial institutions must register on the MoF FATCA/CRS system, follow the onboarding and due diligence procedures, and report reportable accounts to the Ministry every year; the Ministry exchanges the data with the IRS and CRS partners.

references.title: Guidance Notes for the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) United Arab Emirates
references.note: Explains the UAE's widest-approach due diligence, self-certification for new accounts, annual reporting by 30 June after each calendar year, and keeping records for at least five years after the reporting deadline.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Country-by-Country Reporting under Cabinet Resolution 44 of 2020

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | External Audit and CBUAE Examination Readiness

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: The bank, its compliance officers and auditors must immediately report matters of significance and violations to the Central Bank and are protected when reporting in good faith.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Correspondent Banking Relationships under Cabinet Resolution 134 of 2025
programs.why: Before opening a correspondent relationship a bank must refuse shell banks, understand the respondent's business, reputation and supervision, assess its controls, obtain senior management approval and agree responsibilities, with extra checks on payable-through accounts. Staff in these roles need this competence; training is covered by the general AML/CFT programme duty.

references.title: Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 on the Executive Regulations of Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 on AML/CFT/CPF
references.note: Sets the due diligence steps before entering a correspondent relationship, including the shell bank ban, assessing respondent controls, senior management approval and payable-through account checks.

references.title: Guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions on Correspondent Banking and Expectations for Managing Risks
references.note: CBUAE guidance on risk-based management of correspondent relationships.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Trade Finance and Dual-Use Goods Screening
programs.why: EOCN guidance treats trade finance as a higher proliferation financing risk: banks should check trade documents against the UAE Control List, seek end-use information and confirm permits for dual-use goods, and staff in critical compliance and audit roles for trade finance should get additional PF training. This is guidance, so it is classified as a competence expectation.

references.title: Guidance on Counter Proliferation Financing for FIs, DNFBPs, and VASPs
references.provision: Trade Finance and Dual-Use Goods; Training and Education for Staff; Section 6
references.note: Expects screening of trade documents against the UAE Control List, extra due diligence on dual-use goods and additional PF training for compliance and audit staff handling higher-risk products such as trade finance.

references.title: Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 on the Executive Regulations of Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 on AML/CFT/CPF
references.note: Internal controls must include periodic programmes to build the capacity of compliance staff and other relevant employees.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | New Products and Emerging Technologies: Risk Assessment Before Launch
programs.why: Banks must assess ML/TF/PF risks of new products, delivery channels and technologies before launch, and the 2025 law brings any financial activity offered through emerging technologies such as DeFi platforms under CBUAE licensing. Product and innovation staff must be competent in these requirements; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 on the Executive Regulations of Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 on AML/CFT/CPF
references.note: Risks of new products, business practices, delivery mechanisms and technologies must be identified and assessed before launch, with mitigating measures.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Any licensed financial activity carried out through emerging technologies, platforms or protocols falls under CBUAE licensing and oversight.

references.title: Guidelines for Financial Institutions Adopting Enabling Technologies
references.note: Joint supervisory guidelines on risk management for APIs, cloud, biometrics, big data, AI and distributed ledgers.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services
programs.why: CBUAE guidance expects governance, accountability, explainability, fairness, human oversight and third-party controls for AI, read with the Model Management Standards. It is guidance and could not be opened for automated checking, so this is recorded as good practice.

references.title: Guidance Note on the Consumer Protection and Responsible Adoption and Use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning by Licensed Financial Institutions in the U.A.E.
references.note: Guidance on AI governance, fairness, transparency, human oversight, data privacy and third-party AI providers.

references.title: Guidelines for Financial Institutions Adopting Enabling Technologies
references.note: Includes expectations on governance and accountability for big data analytics and AI.

programs.title: United Arab Emirates | Open Finance under the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation
programs.why: Open finance is a licensed financial activity under the 2025 law, and the Open Finance Regulation sets up a central API hub and trust framework with banks among the first participants. Staff building or running data-sharing and payment initiation services must know the consent, security and liability rules. The CBUAE Rulebook could not be opened for automated checking, so the Rulebook reference is unchecked.

references.title: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 Regarding the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business
references.issuer: UAE Federal Government (text published by the Ministry of Finance)
references.note: Lists providing open finance services as a licensed financial activity.

references.title: Open Finance Regulation
references.note: Sets out licensing and operation of the open finance framework, with banks and insurers onboarded in the first phase.

notes: Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 replaced Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 from 14 October 2025. It makes proliferation financing a standalone offence, raises penalties and strengthens senior management accountability.

Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 replaced Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 (as amended) as the AML/CFT/CPF executive regulations from 14 December 2025. Older CBUAE guidance still cites article numbers from the 2019 decision; the compliance officer training duty is now Article 22(4) of the 2025 resolution.

Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 on the Central Bank, financial institutions and insurance replaced Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 from 16 September 2025. It does not apply in the financial free zones.

The CBUAE Operational Risk Management Regulation (Circular 1/2026), effective 14 September 2026, repealed the 2018 Operational Risk Regulation and adds operational resilience, third-party risk and annual continuity testing requirements.

The CBUAE reissued several AML/CFT/CPF guidance papers in late 2025 (CDD/KYC and record keeping, correspondent banking, role-based training best practices) to align with the new law; the 2021 AML/CFT Guidelines remain in the Rulebook but predate the 2025 law.
Cabinet Resolution 74 of 2020 remains the TFS framework; the Cabinet periodically approves updated UAE terrorist lists under it. The EOCN amended its TFS guidance most recently in March 2026.

Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 keeps existing CBUAE regulations, standards and circulars in force until replaced (Article 183) and gave institutions one year from entry into force to align with it (Article 184). It adds explicit duties on fraud prevention, a ban on compound interest and qualified staff for regulatory reporting.

The CBUAE Rulebook lists a new Open Finance Regulation (Circular 3/2025) replacing the 2023 version, a Credit Risk Management Regulation issued in 2024, and a February 2026 guidance note on responsible use of AI and machine learning; these could not be opened for automated checking.

The Corporate Tax law (Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022) was last amended by Federal Decree-Law No. 28 of 2025, effective 15 October 2025; the Ministry of Finance also publishes a page on the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) alongside FATCA and CRS.
